conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having this gnawing pain in my stomach, mostly at night. It wakes me up. And I’ve been feeling more swollen, especially in my right leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any shortness of breath or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a little. Especially when I walk. And I’ve had low-grade fevers, but no chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned swelling. How much weight have you gained?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m usually 110 pounds. Now I’m up to 115. I’ve already increased my torsemide, but it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll check your labs and do a chest X-ray to see if you’re holding extra fluid in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also had nausea this morning after taking Ultram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on that for now. Let’s focus on the pain and swelling first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows mild fluid buildup in your lungs. That explains the shortness of breath. We’ll start IV furosemide to help you lose the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help my leg swelling too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should. But your right leg swelling is worse than the left, which makes us think it’s related to your bypass surgery. We did an ultrasound — no blood clot, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But the stomach pain is still bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. You have a history of pneumatosis intestinalis. That, plus the nighttime pain after eating, makes us concerned about mesenteric ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s reduced blood flow to the intestines, similar to how heart disease causes chest pain. Eating can make it worse because the gut needs more blood to digest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been having pain after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on sucralfate and omeprazole to protect your stomach. But we may switch back to ranitidine because it doesn’t interfere with your tacrolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I take a lot of transplant meds. I don’t want anything messing with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re being very careful. Your tacrolimus level came back at 4.1, which is acceptable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been passing more urine since the IV diuretics. How’s your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I can lie flat now without gasping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re adding a new pill called metolazone. It works with your diuretics to remove more fluid. Take it about an hour before your torsemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I keep this after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. We’ll adjust based on how you do. Your heart function was checked with an echo — it’s still around 25-30%, which is your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my heart isn’t getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks stable. The shortness of breath was mostly from fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile since admission. We checked blood cultures, CMV, and EBV — all negative. No sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having night sweats though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not concerned about serious causes like lymphoma. It could be related to your history or medications. If it continues, your PCP can evaluate further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with your gastroenterologist. They agree your symptoms point to mesenteric ischemia. No immediate procedure, but you’ll need follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What can I do to manage the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eat smaller, more frequent meals. Avoid heavy exercise after eating. Keep taking your laxatives to prevent straining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ranitidine — will I stay on that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve switched back to ranitidine and sucralfate. Omeprazole can raise tacrolimus levels, so it’s safer this way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Creatinine is 3.3, which is expected with your kidney history. White count is low but unchanged — likely from your immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level. We’re watching it. No signs of infection, so we’re not concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my warfarin? I usually take 5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was high — 5.5 — so we held warfarin. We’ll restart at 4 mg when you go home. Check your INR tomorrow and follow up with your doctor in 2–3 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. Any other changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your torsemide to 100 mg twice daily. It was 150 mg, but with metolazone, we can lower it to reduce side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leg swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with TED stockings. They’ll help with the swelling and prevent skin breakdown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Breathing is easier, and the pain is less intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re giving you morphine for breakthrough pain. Take it only if needed, every 8 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should weigh myself every morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day. That could mean fluid is building up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep your GI and cardiology follow-ups. We’ll send all the details to your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — should I avoid flying?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. But stay hydrated and move your legs if you do travel. Best to wait until your swelling improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here to help. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and meds before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when they are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed, but I hope you keep improving at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Press the call button if you need anything before discharge.
